tier_reason: Upgraded from B under the wave's GPU-kernel precedent (FA3 retier-01, sgemm.cu): the paper PDF in the repo (assets/fa4_paper.pdf) gives FA4 vs cuDNN 9.13.0 and 9.19.1.2 TFLOPs/s on a named GPU (B200) with the toolchain (CUDA 13.1, CuTe-DSL 4.4.1, PyTorch 2.10.0, Triton 3.6, FA 2.8.3) and timing method (5 warmup, 10 repeats averaged), and the public harness benchmarks/benchmark_attn.py times FA4 and cuDNN (fwd and bwd) with defaults that match the paper (total 32k tokens, 16 heads at head dim 128, warmup 5, rep 10). Compile options are fixed in public source (flash_attn/cute/interface.py: cute.compile options '--enable-tvm-ffi' plus per-kernel ptxas_options).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper abstract: 'up to 1.3x speedup over cuDNN 9.13 and 2.7x over Triton on B200 GPUs with BF16, reaching up to 1613 TFLOPs/s (71% utilization)'. Figure 4 (forward, head dim 128, TFLOPs/s, seq 1K/2K/4K/8K/16K/32K): non-causal FA4 1355, 1468, 1532, 1579, 1601, 1613; cuDNN 9.13.0 1157, 1328, 1413, 1460, 1488, 1517 (FA4 1.06-1.17x, derived from page data); cuDNN 9.19.1.2 1346, 1474, 1552, 1585, 1609, 1613 (0.99-1.01x, derived); Triton 3.6.0 507 to 703 (FA4 2.29-2.67x, derived); FA2 383 to 432. Causal FA4 744, 1053, 1279, 1426, 1526, 1576; cuDNN 9.13.0 717, 929, 1076, 1168, 1285, 1266 (1.04-1.24x, derived); cuDNN 9.19.1 822, 1103, 1295, 1430, 1509, 1540 (0.91-1.02x, derived: cuDNN ahead up to 8K); Triton 351 to 670 (2.12-2.36x, derived). Figure 5 (forward causal, head dim 192/128): FA4 812, 1121, 1357, 1506, 1600, 1654 vs cuDNN 9.13.0 769, 999, 1167, 1276, 1375, 1382 (1.06-1.20x, derived) vs cuDNN 9.19.1.2 860, 1133, 1311, 1415, 1515, 1563 (0.94-1.06x, derived). Figure 6 (backward, head dim 128): non-causal FA4 936, 1166, 1331, 1430, 1457, 1412 vs cuDNN 9.13.0 857, 1016, 1116, 1171, 1212, 1107 (1.09-1.28x, derived) vs cuDNN 9.19.1.2 928, 1108, 1231, 1300, 1280, 1274 (1.01-1.14x, derived); causal FA4 614, 887, 1102, 1284, 1402, 1446 vs cuDNN 9.13.0 543, 732, 893, 1008, 1085, 1142 (1.13-1.29x, derived) vs cuDNN 9.19.1 651, 894, 1090, 1218, 1293, 1337 (0.94-1.08x, derived). So the 'up to 1.3x over cuDNN 9.13' is reached only in the backward pass (forward peaks at 1.24x), and the only remaining lead over current cuDNN 9.19 is in the backward pass at long sequences (up to about 1.14x).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Paper Appendix A.1: CUDA 13.1, CuTe-DSL 4.4.1, PyTorch 2.10.0, Triton 3.6, FlashAttention 2.8.3, cuDNN 9.13 and 9.19.1.2; 5 warmup runs then 10 repeats averaged. CuTe-DSL kernels are JIT compiled; compile options are fixed in flash_attn/cute/interface.py (cute.compile options '--enable-tvm-ffi', plus a kernel's ptxas_options where set). HEAD's flash_attn/cute/pyproject.toml now requires nvidia-cutlass-dsl>=4.6.2, so a HEAD build does not match the paper's CuTe-DSL 4.4.1.
corrections.caveats: Paper read from the PDF checked into the repo (assets/fa4_paper.pdf); arXiv, the MLSys proceedings page, the Together AI blog and the Colfax post were not opened (egress-blocked), so the peer-review status rests on a search result and was not checked by me. The Figure 4 caption itself says 'newer versions of cuDNN have incorporated many of the techniques described in this paper, yielding similar performance to FA4', and Appendix A.1 says the authors worked with the cuDNN team to fold FA4 techniques into cuDNN from 9.13/9.14 on: in the forward pass FA4 is at parity with cuDNN 9.19.1.2 (and behind it at short causal sequences, e.g. 744 vs 822 TFLOPs/s at 1K causal), and the 1.1-1.3x lead holds only against cuDNN 9.13.0; in the backward pass FA4 still leads cuDNN 9.19 by up to about 1.14x at long sequences (derived from page data). The forward figures alone peak at 1.24x over cuDNN 9.13, so the abstract's 'up to 1.3x' comes from the backward pass. Figure 5 shows 1654 TFLOPs/s at head dim 192/128, above the abstract's 'up to 1613'. Appendix inconsistencies: it names a 'B100 180GB SXM6 (1000W)' while the text and every figure say B200 (180 GB and 1000 W match B200), and it dates the library versions to 'March 2025', which cannot be right for CUDA 13.1. The public harness covers FA2, FA3, FA4, cuDNN and PyTorch standard attention but not the Triton or Gluon baselines, and no tag marks the commit used for the paper's figures. FlashAttention-3 'does not run on B200' (paper footnote), so there is no FA4 vs FA3 comparison, and the paper has no H100 FA4 numbers. Several authors are from NVIDIA and Colfax, and the cuDNN team is thanked for feedback. Shares the Dao-AILab/flash-attention repository with FlashAttention-3 (use id paper:flashattention-4).

notes: All Figure 4 bar labels in the record match the PDF exactly (checked at 330 dpi). Upgraded to A by the same reasoning the orchestrator used for FA3 (public harness + stated toolchain + named GPU); keep at B if the orchestrator prefers to require a pinned commit. Worth recording: the lead over current cuDNN (9.19) is forward parity and backward up to 1.14x only.

tier_reason: The PR's independent measurements (slaren on M3 Max, max-krasnyansky on M4 Pro and Galaxy S25, rmatif on Galaxy A34) mostly show KleidiAI equal to or slower than llama.cpp's own Arm kernels; the only independent win is the SME path at 1-2 threads on M4 Pro (about 1.28-1.30x). The numbers showing a general win come from Arm: the PR author's Pixel 8 table (1.03-1.19x) and the later Arm-authored PR #24414 (SME2 F32, no test name or build flags), so the evidence for 'faster' is first-party with partial methodology.

corrections.claimed_speedup: llama.cpp PR #11390 (Arm-authored integration, merged 2025-02-20). Independent runs: max-krasnyansky (Qualcomm org member), Apple M4 Pro, llama 1B Q4_0, master vs KleidiAI SME: 1 thread pp128 160.94 vs 205.39, tg64 47.84 vs 62.22 (about 1.28x and 1.30x, derived from page data); 2 threads pp128 312.10 vs 389.43, tg64 87.31 vs 99.95; 4 threads pp128 586.83 vs 326.86, tg64 157.63 vs 110.52; 10 threads pp128 1173.93 vs 435.39, tg64 243.65 vs 162.36. KleidiAI I8MM on M4 Pro: 162.40, 304.78, 531.04, 1082.70 pp128 (equal or slower). Galaxy S25 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) 1 thread pp128 181.23 master vs 174.13 KleidiAI. slaren, M3 Max, llama 7B Q4_0, 12 threads: pp128 229.89 master vs 192.93 PR, tg32 31.54 vs 30.54 (slower). rmatif, Galaxy A34: pp512 84.25 master vs 87.11 PR, tg128 13.79 vs 11.00. First-party (chaxu01, Arm), Pixel 8, llama 7B Q4_0: pp512 19.33/37.59/69.59 master vs 20.48/40.40/74.00 PR at 1/2/4 threads, tg128 9.75/18.48/27.42 vs 11.58/21.40/28.27 (about 1.03-1.19x, derived). Comments as extracted: max-krasnyansky 'SME does much better on 1 and 2 threads and much worse from then on' and 'It looks like even Kleidi I8MM kernels perform worse than what we have in the master'; chaxu01 (Arm) 'KleidiAI's performance is generally comparable to the current AARCH64 kernels. However, we have observed performance degradation when using a high number of threads on hardware with high core count.' The record's quoted 'PR summary' ('KleidiAI SME excels with 1-2 threads but degrades significantly at higher core counts. I8MM kernels consistently underperform') was not found on the page. Later first-party claim, PR #24414 (chaxu01, merged 2026-07-14): SME2 F32 vs native F32 on Apple M4 Pro, Llama-3.2-1B F32, 19.70 vs 457.57 t/s at 1 thread up to 23.6x at 2 threads, 4.3x at 6 threads; test name and build flags not stated.
corrections.hardware: PR #11390: Apple M4 Pro and Samsung Galaxy S25 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) run by max-krasnyansky (member of the Qualcomm GitHub org); Apple M3 Max (12 threads) by slaren; Galaxy A34 by rmatif; Google Pixel 8 by the PR author chaxu01 (Arm). PR #24414: Apple M4 Pro (Arm author).
corrections.license: Apache-2.0 (the LICENSES directory also carries BSD-3-Clause.txt for some files)
corrections.caveats: First-party vs independent: the PR #11390 author is chaxu01 (Charles Xu; GitHub profile company 'Arm', Lund), so the integration and the Pixel 8 numbers are Arm's own; the M4 Pro, S25, M3 Max and A34 tables were posted by people outside Arm (max-krasnyansky is a member of the Qualcomm GitHub org, slaren is a ggml maintainer), and those independent tables mostly show KleidiAI slower than llama.cpp's own Arm kernels. Arm's own comment in the PR calls KleidiAI 'generally comparable' to those kernels, with degradation at high thread counts; on 2025-02-05 Arm noted that max-krasnyansky's runs lacked commit f4eb1b3 (multithreaded LHS packing), and on 2025-02-19 said the kernels 'are currently optimized for lower thread counts', so the scaling issue was still present at merge. The baseline is llama.cpp's own ggml Arm Q4_0 kernels, not a library on the project's baseline list (oneDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen). The later SME2 F32 claim (PR #24414: 4.3-23.6x vs ggml's native F32 path) is Arm-authored, gives no test name, build flags or BLAS/Accelerate setting, and no reviewer reproduced it. The KleidiAI README and the GitHub mirror carry no comparative figures; Arm's blog claims (ExecuTorch, MediaPipe, XNNPACK) were not opened. Values were read through WebFetch page extraction; the four headline M4 Pro values were consistent across three fetches. The PR conversation had 11 hidden items that WebFetch could not load. The GitHub repo is a read-only mirror of gitlab.arm.com/kleidi/kleidiai. Numbers are dated: KleidiAI and its llama.cpp integration changed substantially since (SME2 kernels, runtime kernel selection, dynamic scheduling in PR #23819).

notes: Answer to the orchestrator: the PR is Arm-authored (chaxu01, profile company Arm), but the measurements the record cites were posted by non-Arm contributors (a Qualcomm org member and rmatif), and they show KleidiAI mostly not faster than llama.cpp's own kernels; Arm's own PR numbers are small wins. Downgraded to C; a shortcoming worth recording is 'independent llama.cpp measurements mostly slower than llama.cpp's own Arm kernels; wins only with SME at 1-2 threads'. The record's quoted 'PR summary' sentence was not found on the page.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed paper (ICML 2025, per the README) whose Figure 2 (README image, RTX 4090) and Table 1 (assets/exp_table.png) show SpargeAttn ahead of FlashAttention2 / full attention in kernel TOPS and per-layer speed, with accuracy metrics. Not A: no kernel benchmark script in the repo (Triton_SpargeAttn holds only triton_kernel_example.py; evaluate/ holds model examples), and no compiler or flags are stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Table 1 (assets/exp_table.png), average per-layer speed in TOPS, Full-Attention vs SpargeAttn (sparsity): Llama3.1 128K 156.9 vs 708.1 (0.54); CogvideoX 17K 166.0 vs 507.9 (0.46); Mochi 22K 164.2 vs 582.4 (0.47); Flux 4.5K 158.2 vs 280.3 (0.38); Stable-Diffusion3.5 4.5K 164.2 vs 293.0 (0.31); about 4.5x, 3.1x, 3.5x, 1.8x and 1.8x (derived from page data). Accuracy stays near dense (e.g. Llama3.1 WikiText perplexity 6.020 vs 6.013; Mochi CLIPSIM 0.1720 vs 0.1725). Figure 2 (assets/speed_comparison.png, RTX 4090, seq 22K, head dim 128; values read from the chart, approximate): FlashAttn about 165 TOPS flat; SageAttn about 300 flat; SpargeAttn+Sage2 about 410 at sparsity 0.1 rising to about 875 at 0.6 (about 2.5-5.3x over FlashAttn, derived); SpargeAttn+Sage about 320 to 675; SpargeAttn+FA2 about 183 at 0.1 to about 370 at 0.6 (about 1.1-2.2x, derived).

notes: Numbers in the record match the two images. Worth recording: most of the headline gain over FlashAttention2 comes from SageAttention's INT8 quantization (SageAttn alone is about 1.8x FlashAttn in Figure 2), with sparsity adding the rest; at sparsity 0.1 the FA2-based variant is only about 1.1x.
